items.note: Udayapur praśasti records Vākpati's victory over the Karnāṭa army, though early victories could not break the Cālukyas.
Muñja fell captive to Tailapa and was executed; tradition preserved by Merutuṅga's Muñja-Prabandha.
Merutuṅga's version of Vākpati's overthrow corroborated by the Kauthem grant, Gadag inscription and Āʾīn-i-Akbarī.
Amitagati's work of 993 A.D. names Muñja as reigning; Tailapa II died shortly before 998, so Muñja's execution falls between these dates.
Vākpati a poet and patron who brought a renaissance of Sanskrit literature; excavated tanks (Muñjasāgara at Dhārā) and built temples and embankments.
Succession passed to Sindhurāja; the Prabandhas claim Bhoja directly succeeded Muñja after a feud, a point disputed in the next chunk.
At least five dynastic inscriptions show Sindhurāja immediately succeeded Vākpati, with no hint of enmity.
Sindhurāja's titles Kumāranārāyaṇa and Navasāhasāṅka; no inscription of his reign yet found; main source is Padmagupta.

items.note: Sindhurāja fostered the literary movement; Padmagupta's poetic genius revived under his patronage; Dhanika and Dhanapāla at his court.
Taking Merutuṅga's 55 years 7 months 3 days, Bhoja's accession is placed in early 999 A.D.; Lassen and Bühler differ.
Contemporary records show Vākpati succeeded by Sindhurāja, then Bhoja; six inscriptions of Bhoja's reign known.
Sarasvatī image inscription of 1033 A.D.: Bhoja had the image of Vāgdevī erected by a sculptor, Manathala.
Betma plates of 1020 A.D.: Bhoja grants village Nālataḍāga to a learned Brahman for religious merit of king and parents.
Kalvan inscription: land, two oil-mills, fourteen shops and fourteen drammas donated to a temple.
Al-Bīrūnī: Bhilsa the eastern limit of Malwa in 1030 A.D.; outline of Bhoja's dominion.
Bhoja rebuilt Dhārā on a new model and transferred his capital there from Ujjain.
Bhoja renowned for literary and architectural achievements.
